newsitem.title: GERMANY: TNT chief sees express revenue falling.
newsitem.headline: TNT chief sees express revenue falling.

text.p: Express freight revenue per shipment could fall up to five percent annually over the coming years through growing competition, a leading express operator forecast.
John Fellows, chief executive officer of global freight integrator TNT Express Worldwide, said more mergers and acquisitions would come as small companies were squeezed out of the European market.

Only the big integrators could invest enough to meet customer demands for a full range of transport services, real-time information technology and added-value services, he told the eighth World Express & Mail conference in Frankfurt.
"Rates will be driven down by the combined force of customers and major suppliers so that average revenue per shipment will continue to decline by as much as four to five percent annually," he said.

"What we will see will be more consolidation as smaller companies are squeezed out of the market or acquired by bigger operators wanting their specialist expertise and their regional networks," Fellows predicted.
Road transport in Europe and the Americas and air transport in Asia would be the top growth markets, he added.
TNT, following its takeover by Dutch post and telecoms group KPN at the start of the year, could now strengthen its pan-European parcels service within its global distribution network, he added.

Real-time access to tracking systems would be demanded by customers and nearly three percent of worldwide TNT consignments were now tracked in its Internet Web Tracker service after just four months in operation, Fellows said.

"I am sure that in time, using the internet or other forms of non-personal contact for booking, pick-up, delivery or billing enquiries rather than calling to speak to an operator will become the norm," he added.
Paul Jackson, chief executive of conference organiser Triangle Management Services, forecast global logistics companies would emerge as suppliers to the global corporate supply chain.
In addition to integrators, freight forwarders and air cargo specialists, these could include IT firms, autonomous logistics departments of large corporations and shipping lines, he forecast.
Non-transport industry entrants could include IBM, General Electric and Caterpillar, Jackson noted.
